meta.title: Function Calling and Tool Use
meta.thesis: Function calling and tool use connect models to APIs through typed tool declarations; the model proposes a call, while the runtime validates, authorizes, executes, and returns the result.

mentalMap.title: Function calling — model proposes, code executes
mentalMap.caption: The flow separates tool schema, model-selected arguments, runtime execution, and result handling.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Function calling lets a model request external capabilities, but application code owns validation, authorization, execution, and side effects.

modules.title: A tool is an action boundary
modules.sub: Start by separating model text from application action.
modules.summary: Function calling does not let a model magically access systems. It lets the model request a named action that code may accept or reject.
objectives: Distinguish model proposal from code execution.
Name safe and risky tool categories.

blocks.title: The model asks; code decides

spans.text: A tool call is a structured request: a name plus arguments. The model can propose `lookup_order(order_id="A123")`, but it does not hold credentials or execute the database query itself.
Problem anchor: a support bot needs order status and refund actions. Looking up an order is mostly read-only; issuing a refund changes money and needs stronger authorization.
Before reading on, predict: which tool needs stricter checks, `lookup_order` or `issue_refund`? Why?

blocks.analogy: A tool call is like a purchase request: filling the form is not the same as approving the spend.

blocks.title: Case study: order lookup versus refund

spans.text: The support assistant receives: “Where is order A123, and refund it if late.” It should call `lookup_order` first. It should not call `issue_refund` until policy and user confirmation are checked.

items.text: Read-only tool: lower risk but still validates order ID.
Side-effecting tool: requires policy, confirmation, and audit log.
Final answer: explains what happened and what still needs approval.

blocks.title: Check the boundary

options.text: Application runtime code after validation and authorization.

blocks.explanation: The model proposes calls; code owns execution.

modules.title: Tool schemas shape model choices
modules.sub: After the boundary, define names and arguments precisely.
modules.summary: The model chooses tools from declarations. Clear names, descriptions, and input schemas reduce wrong-tool and missing-argument failures.

blocks.title: Names and descriptions are model-facing UX

spans.text: Tool declarations include a name, description, and input schema. The model reads those declarations as part of context, so vague names and overlapping descriptions make selection harder.
A good tool schema says what the tool does, when to use it, what arguments are required, and what the tool does not do.

blocks.analogy: Tool descriptions are labels on drawers; confusing labels make the model open the wrong drawer.

spans.text: Tool name: `lookup_order`. Description: “Fetch shipping and payment status for one order ID. Does not issue refunds.” Input schema: `{order_id: string}` required. Output: status, delivery date, refundable flag.
That “does not issue refunds” sentence matters. It tells the model not to treat a lookup tool as an action tool.

blocks.title: Check schemas
blocks.prompt: Why include “does not issue refunds” in lookup_order?

options.text: To make the database query faster.
To prevent wrong-tool selection when the user asks for a refund.
To hide the refund tool from code.

blocks.explanation: Tool descriptions guide model selection; boundaries should be explicit.

modules.title: Validate and execute outside the model
modules.sub: A proposed call becomes real only after code checks it.
modules.summary: Runtime code validates arguments, checks authorization, executes the function, handles errors, and records the action.
objectives: Reject unknown tools and missing arguments.
Explain why authorization lives in code.

blocks.title: Execution is runtime responsibility

spans.text: The application should treat tool calls as untrusted input. It validates the tool name against an allowed registry, checks arguments against schema, enforces policy, then executes.
This division is what makes tool use safe enough to ship: the model can reason about actions, but code owns permissions and side effects.

blocks.analogy: The runtime is the cashier who checks the form, not the person who casually suggested buying something.

blocks.title: Execute only known safe tools

spans.text: Run this as a tiny model of the mechanism. The point is to predict behavior before trusting the output.

It prints:
late
True

The runtime accepts a known tool with the required argument and returns structured data.

syntax.explains: The small concrete case the example operates on.
The line or function that turns the inputs into behavior.
A visible result so you can check your prediction.

spans.text: When an AI writes tool-calling code, check the dangerous boundary.

items.text: Does it reject unknown tool names?
Does it validate required arguments before execution?
Does it separate read-only and side-effecting permissions?
Does it log tool name, arguments, result, and errors?

modules.title: Return results for the next decision
modules.sub: Once code runs, the model needs the result as new evidence.
modules.summary: Tool results should be tied to the original call and treated as untrusted context. The model uses them to continue or answer.
objectives: Treat tool output as data, not instructions.

blocks.title: Tool output re-enters context as evidence

spans.text: After execution, the application sends the tool result back to the model, usually tied to the tool-call ID. The model can then decide whether to answer, call another tool, or ask for approval.
Tool output is not privileged instruction. A web page, database note, or document can contain malicious text. Label it as data and keep higher-priority instructions separate.

blocks.analogy: A tool result is a receipt; useful evidence, not a new boss.

blocks.title: Case study: late order refund flow

spans.text: Turn 1: model calls `lookup_order(A123)`. Runtime returns status late, refundable true. Turn 2: model wants `issue_refund`, but runtime requires confirmation and policy check. The assistant asks the user to confirm instead of silently refunding.
The important handoff is that the lookup result becomes evidence, not permission.

blocks.title: Check results
blocks.prompt: How should the app treat tool output text?

options.text: As higher-priority instructions than system policy.
As untrusted data that can inform the next step.
As proof that the final action is authorized.

blocks.explanation: Tool outputs can contain useful facts or malicious text; code and policy still govern.

modules.title: Failure modes and safe tool use
modules.sub: End with how tool loops break in practice.
modules.summary: Tool systems fail through wrong tools, malformed arguments, unsafe side effects, stale results, and prompt injection in tool output.

blocks.title: How function calling breaks

spans.text: Function calling failures often look like normal agent behavior until a real system is changed. The model may choose the wrong tool, omit arguments, retry blindly, or trust malicious tool output.

items.text: Wrong tool: search instead of order lookup, or refund instead of lookup.
Malformed arguments: missing ID, wrong enum, bad date.
Unauthorized side effect: sending, deleting, charging, or refunding without approval.
Tool-output injection: retrieved text tells the model to ignore policy.

blocks.analogy: Tool failure is like giving a helpful intern access to the company credit card without purchase controls.

blocks.useWhen: Let the model call a tool when it lacks live data or needs a deterministic capability that code can validate.
blocks.avoidWhen: Do not execute side-effecting tools when arguments are incomplete, approval is missing, output is untrusted, or policy is ambiguous.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: The model may choose; code must verify; humans approve irreversible actions.

blocks.title: Check safe tool use
blocks.prompt: What is the safest rule for irreversible tools?

options.text: Let the model decide based on confidence.
Require explicit policy checks and confirmation in code before execution.
Hide tool results from the model.

blocks.explanation: Irreversible actions need authorization outside the model.
